items.text: Leigh lifted weights, walked 10,000 steps a day and still gained 50kg. Her weight loss story shows why 'eat less, move more' isn't always the answer
items.article: Leigh was strength training four times a week, walking 10K steps a day, yet the scales kept climbing. After doctors repeatedly told her to exercise more, a shocking photo forced her to search for answers. For a long time, Leigh Woods avoided paying too much attention to her reflection. At 110kg, she didn't particularly like looking at herself in the mirror and had become good at avoiding it. Then she spotted a side-on photograph of herself in a workplace newsletter. 'I was just like, "Oh, is that what I look like? I need to do something about it,"' the 35-year-old, from Sydney , tells the Daily Mail. By then, Leigh's confidence had taken a hit. She was going out less and didn't particularly want to be seen. Even her motivation was beginning to suffer, although she was still getting herself to the gym. That was the part she couldn't understand. Leigh wasn't someone who had stopped exercising as her weight climbed. She was strength training four mornings a week, aiming for 10,000 steps a day and fitting in cardio sessions, while also paying attention to her nutrition. Yet she estimates she was gaining around 10kg a year. After years of trying to shift it, Leigh had started wondering whether the problem was her. 'Am I actually doing what I'm meant to be doing?' she remembers thinking. 'Am I just lying to myself? Should I just add in more exercise?'

In a TikTok, the 25-year-old shared: “Somebody once said to me, ‘Lola, there will be a day when you wake up, you’ll be 25 or 26, from a deep sleep, and you’ll start to feel the effects of vaping’... The day has come. “My lungs feel like they’re battery-powered, like they’re just one big battery. “Breathing feels like a chore; it feels like hard work, it feels like I should be paid for breathing. It feels like there will be no tomorrow”. Speaking to HuffPost UK, Girish Desai , Chief Pharmacist at Landys Chemist , said that while “Vaping is less harmful than smoking and can be a useful way for smokers to quit cigarettes... we should not confuse less harmful with harmless”. Though the NHS’s site agrees that it’s a better alternative than smoking, they also say it’s “not harmless” and that we still don’t know what its long-term effects might be. They added that kids and non-smokers should “never” vape. Meanwhile, a Nature article suggests that those who begin vaping as children might see “bigger health risks than we’d thought”, with potential lung issues “just the tip of the iceberg”.

Celebrity fans include Maya Jama, who shares her clinic sessions, and actress Hailey Bieber, who told Time magazine: "I swear by them." Whether there is a physical change - or any need for one - is debatable, but fans of the massages claim they help "flatten" and "debloat" and give a "snatched waist" and "sculpted abs". Many videos on social media promoting lymphatic massage show a woman either standing sideways, facing the front or perhaps lying down with her stomach showing a slight - and very normal - curve outwards. items.text: Wolf encounter: A photographer on what humans have lost
items.article: How a brush with the wild can expose what modern life no longer asks of us. This article is part of a series in which we speak to individuals who – due to a unique job, location or experience – share an insight they wish others could know. What’s the one thing people should know? Modern life has reduced how often we are truly required to meet the world on its own terms — until we encounter something that refuses to adapt to us. It lasted only a few minutes, but Norwegian wildlife photographer Lasse Huldt Pedersen remembers his closest encounter with a wolf in meticulous detail. Wolves usually smell humans long before they see them, but on a late summer day in 2022, Pedersen believes the wind carried his scent away from the apex predator, allowing them to come nearly face-to-face. As he stood quietly among the pine trees in eastern Norway near the Swedish border, patiently waiting to spot a wolf, one appeared on a rocky rise above him. The animal scanned the forest, turning its head several times before it finally sensed him. When the wolf locked onto Pedersen, it held firm eye contact, deliberately lowering its head while standing tall on the rocky outcrop — a typical feature in Scandinavia due to Ice Age glacial erosion.

items.text: Science Explains Why You May Have 'Jelly Legs' After Exercise
items.article: Some shakiness after exercising is typical, but there’s a critical difference between “jello legs” and feeling sore and hurt days later. There’s a rite of passage when you start a new exercise routine or sport: following your workout, parts of your body may wobble like jelly. While this experience can happen even with pros, Andrew Jagim , an exercise physiologist at the University of Wisconsin, said that “jelly legs” are especially common with beginners who are not used to working out. “Even doing body-weight squats for five minutes could be enough to make their legs start shaking and quivering,” he said. Even though this is a natural physiological reaction, it’s still something you’ll want to watch. Unsteady muscles after you use your maximum effort are part of your body’s cry for some rest. From an athletic trainer’s perspective, the signal means: “Hey, it’s time to sit down. Don’t go hurt yourself,” said Patrick Maloney , the lead athletic trainer at Tulane Institute of Sports Medicine in New Orleans. When this physical shakiness occurs, it means your nerves are short-circuiting and are having trouble communicating with your muscles, Jagim said, because of the rapid onset of fatigue your training is causing. So your body “can’t initiate muscle contraction and relaxing like it normally does,” Jagim explained.

One of the best-known meteor showers is now active until 7 November. The Orionids are particularly fast and can leave trails in the sky that last a few seconds after the meteor itself has gone. The display occurs at around the same time each year when the Earth passes through a trail of dust and debris left behind by Halley's Comet. The showers peak overnight from 21 to 22 October. The Orionids are particularly fast, entering the atmosphere at around 41 miles per second. items.text: I’m a pharmacist — these are five surprising flu symptoms you might not know
items.article: A superintendent pharmacist has highlighted lesser-known signs as cases rise. A sudden high temperature, body aches and a sore throat are commons symptoms of flu that many of us are all too familiar with. But as the temperature drops and respiratory infections start to climb, Claire Nevinson, superintendent pharmacist at Boots, has highlighted some lesser-known symptoms. She said: “Flu, also known as influenza, is a common viral infection that spreads from person to person. “You can catch it at any time of year, but it’s more common in winter , as we spend more time indoors and around others. It’s a highly infectious illness and is not the same as a common cold. The symptoms of flu tend to come quickly and can feel more severe. Some of the lesser-known symptoms of flu can include loss of appetite, difficulty sleeping, sore eyes, eye pain or light sensitivity. “When you’re unwell, your immune system kicks in and starts producing more white blood cells to help fight off a viral infection. This means your body redirects its energy and resources toward fighting off the viral infection. In some cases, this can result in everyday activities, like eating, to take a backseat. “If you do experience a loss of appetite, it is important to stay hydrated and have well balanced meals to ensure that your body is still getting all the essential nutrients.” Other flu symptoms highlighted by the NHS including feeling tired of exhausted, a dry cough and a headache. items.text: No iced coffee, AirPods in the waiting room or reading notes off your phone: Experts reveal the modern-day habits that are costing you your dream job
items.article: In today's workplace, it seems there could be a whole new set of habits and behaviours that might sway a hiring manager's opinion in seconds - and it all starts with what you're drinking. What might seem like a harmless everyday purchase has found itself at the centre of a fiery online debate: is it ever OK to bring an iced coffee into a job interview? Anyone who has navigated the corporate world will know that the hiring process comes with plenty of unspoken rules, from how you dress to how you carry yourself in the room. Arriving late, having poor body language, badmouthing a former employer or bringing up salary too early are just some of the classic interview mistakes candidates have long been warned about. But in today's workplace, it seems there could be a whole new set of habits and behaviours that might sway a hiring manager's opinion in seconds - and it all starts with what you're drinking. In recent weeks, the internet has been divided over the simple act of bringing an iced coffee into an interview. While some have branded the move 'unprofessional' and a sign of poor time management, others argue that employers should move away from outdated stigmas about what makes someone look professional.

items.key: ai:experts sound alarm over dangerous health trend increasingly affecting men
items.text: Experts sound alarm over dangerous health trend increasingly affecting men
items.article: Sylvester Stallone's bulimia revelation spotlights a rise in eating disorders among men. Experts say looksmaxxing and body image pressures are driving bulimia in boys and men. Brian Pollack, a licensed clinical social worker and certified eating disorders specialist at Hilltop Behavioral Health in Summit, New Jersey, specializes in treating males who struggle with eating disorders, which he said is "highly underreported." Days after Sylvester Stallone revealed his own history with bulimia, experts are highlighting a growing but often overlooked rise in eating disorders among men. The Academy Award-nominated actor, 80, revealed during an interview with The New York Times that he developed an "obsession" with eating habits while prepping for his role in the 1982 movie "Rambo." Stallone said he took pains to appear more "animalistic," drawing inspiration from jaguars and cats. "It became an obsession. Really bad. It got to the point where I became bulimic," he said during the interview. SYLVESTER STALLONE REVEALS SURPRISING HEALTH STRUGGLE BEHIND HIS FAMOUSLY RIPPED PHYSIQUE Bulimia nervosa is an eating disorder marked by episodes of binge-eating — consuming a large amount of food while feeling a loss of control — followed by purging behaviors such as vomiting, excessive use of laxatives or diuretics, fasting or excessive exercise, according to the National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH).
